name: Laugh Society
_comment_id: The folder is `laugh-society-snapchat` and the name is plain 'Laugh
Society', and the two disagreeing is deliberate. The name is the
brand and is what this show is actually called. The id is a key on a
filesystem, and there are already two folders under the Binge heading
beginning laugh-society- that are a DIFFERENT show with a similar
name: one more of them would read as its third look, which is exactly
the thing somebody would edit by mistake. The heading it belongs to
is the one fact that separates them, so the id says it.
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, and the same kind of thing
every one of them is: the heading names the network these frames are
cut FOR and the channel is the show they are cut from, so another
show cutting for the same network is one more folder under it rather
than a heading of its own.
Like all of its neighbours it is a frame fetcher rather than a
thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of vertical
stills comes out, each carrying the sentence that was being said at
the moment it was cut from.
It follows Hall of Femme, which is the pack to read first: the frame
fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the block
at the foot of the frame and every number in that block are that
pack's, stated here in the same numbers. The prose below points at it
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
It decides three things, and all three are about the words. There is
NO CARD - the type is set straight onto the photograph, which no
other pack under this heading does. It is set in Open Sans with a
picked word in Garet, which is a change of face and a change of
COLOUR at once. And the shade that holds it legible is the channel's
own, laid over the bottom third of the picture.
_comment_capture: The same frame fetch every channel under this heading runs, stated in
the same numbers, because it is the same job: the slider opening at
forty and running to two hundred, delivered at the 540x960 vertical
full-screen frame Snapchat is cut for, transcribed, and rewritten
from speech into reported information before anything is set.
What each of these keys does, and what the rewrite refuses to do, is
written out at length in content/README.md, and pointed at from
hall-of-femme/channel.json. Nothing here disagrees with any of it.
`captions` is on: this channel writes on its frames, so the run has
to transcribe the video's voice track for there to be anything to

_comment_framing: The picture is the product, so it is fitted to the canvas centred and
left alone, exactly as it is on every channel beside this one.
min_text_space is zero because it asks how much room is clear BESIDE
the subject for a title to go in, and this title does not go beside
anybody - it lies across the foot of the picture. No frame should be
rejected for failing to leave a column nothing is ever set in.
_comment_scrim: The one piece of furniture this channel has, and the piece that pays
for everything else about it: a shade thrown up from the bottom edge,
over the photograph, reaching a third of the way up the frame.
Every other pack under this heading sets its caption on a solid card,
and the card is what makes the type legible over a photograph nobody
chose the contrast of. This one has no card. Take the shade away and
the same white letters are laid straight onto whatever the still
happens to contain - a blown-out sky, a white shirt, a strip light -
and a drop shadow does not save them, because a shadow separates type
from a background it already contrasts with rather than creating the
contrast. The shade is what creates it, and it does so without
putting a shape between the viewer and the picture: it darkens the
photograph rather than covering it, which is the whole difference
between this look and the card.
A THIRD of the frame, and it is measured rather than chosen. The
block stands 120px off the foot of a 960-tall frame, and a full four
lines of 40px type with the renderer's own 10px between them is 190px
tall, so the top of the longest caption this channel can produce
lands at 310px - just inside the 320px the scrim reaches. Every
caption is therefore covered end to end, and a shorter one is covered
with room to spare. Less than a third and a four-line caption has its
first line hanging in clear picture; much more and the shade stops
reading as the foot of the frame going dark and starts reading as the
picture having been dimmed.
Bottom to top, because that is the direction it is thrown in. `at`
runs 0 at the canvas floor to 1 at the top of the scrim's own span,
so the stops read in the order the eye travels. There is no way to
aim it at an angle and that is deliberate - see `scrim` in
js/channels.js.
It ends on a fully transparent stop rather than on an opacity of its
own, so there is no line anywhere across the picture where the scrim
stops. The middle stop is what keeps the ramp from being a straight
fade: most of the darkening is spent in the bottom half, where the
type actually is, and the top half is the long tail that hides the
join.
It is drawn on the canvas, under the title and over the photograph -
see compose.addScrim - and it is switched by the Gradient button,
which arrives ON because the shade is part of how this channel looks
rather than an effect to go and find. See `branding` at the foot of
this file for why that button does not also reach the backend.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs cut to Hall of Femme's
design. They set their captions on a coloured slab; this one sets
them on the photograph, under the shade above.
That decides the face. A card is a flat ground somebody chose, and it
is what lets Hall of Femme set a 200-weight hairline at caption size
at all. There is no such ground here: the letters are on a
photograph, darkened but still a photograph, with grain and edges and
detail running through them. What that ground asks for is a face with
solid stems and open counters at 40px, which is what Open Sans is -
a humanist sans drawn to be read small, and the same family two of
its neighbours are already set in.
It also decides the shadow. Hall of Femme states none, because a card
does that job completely and a shadow as well would only smear the
inside of it. Here the shadow is half of what holds the type: the
scrim gives the letters a dark ground to sit on and the shadow gives
them an edge against it, and neither is enough alone on a frame that

_comment_face: Open Sans, in the cut this app carries: `open-sans-italic`, which
is the face Determined and Fight Source are also set in. The
family ships as a set of files each carrying its own full name,
and a channel names the exact cut rather than the family - see
the note in the face pack for why 'Open Sans' on its own is
deliberately not a name anything asks for here.
The slant is drawn into the letterforms and the face is
registered at style normal, which is what `family` and `weight`
between them have to say; there is no third field in the font
shorthand this renderer builds, and inventing one would let the
measurement and the draw come apart. See the face pack, and the
long note in killer-bites/channel.json where the same ground is
covered for a family reached by weight instead.
_comment_uppercase: Off. What the user types is what the canvas sets, capital for
capital, and this is the second pack under the heading to say so
- Killer Bites argues it at length and every word of that
argument holds here.
The short version, because the reasons are this pack's as much as
that one's. The captions arrive from the rewrite rather than from
somebody typing them (see backend/narrator.py), so the casing in
the text box is information produced on purpose, and flattening
it at the draw throws away the more considered of the two. And a
line of capitals is a rectangle where a line of mixed case has
ascenders and descenders sticking out of it - word shape is most
of how a sentence is read at a glance on a phone.
There is a reason of this pack's own on top of those. This is the
only channel here whose type is on the photograph rather than on
a card, and mixed case is what makes that survivable: capitals
are one solid band of ink across the frame, which reads as a
graphic laid on the picture, while a mixed-case line has holes in
it that the picture shows through. The scrim is what makes the
letters legible; the casing is what keeps them from looking
stuck on.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so the text
box held the user's own casing all along and the highlight
buttons already offered the words as the canvas would set them
(see the `cased` note in js/text.js).
_comment_color: Pure white, which is the channel's own answer and therefore what
every frame is set in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame
stores no colour of its own until it is given one, and this is
what it falls back to (see state.textColorFor). It is one of the
three in `colors` below, so the white swatch is the one that
shows as chosen on an untouched frame - the swatch is found by
matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White is the default and not one of the two warm colours for the
reason the scrim exists: the shade is a black one, and white is
what is unambiguously legible on it at every size and over every
photograph underneath. The red and the orange are legible on it
too, and are a swatch away, but a caption whose colour has to be
checked against the frame is not a default.
Pure white rather than an off-white, and it is the one colour
here whose exact value matters. An off-white that reads as white
on a monitor is a grey caption on a phone held next to a bright
still, and there is nothing for a true white to be too harsh
against - it is sitting on a deliberately darkened band.
_comment_shadow: Stated, where every other pack under this heading states null,
and the difference is the card. Those channels put their type on
a solid slab in a colour the user picked, which separates it from
the picture completely and leaves a shadow with nothing to do but
smear the inside of the slab. This channel's type is on the
photograph.
So the shadow is doing the job it was invented for, and it is the
second of the two things holding these letters: the scrim gives
them a dark ground and this gives them an edge against it. Both
are needed. On a still that is already dark the scrim buys
little and the shadow is the whole of the separation; on a bright
one the shadow alone would be a soft grey halo round white
letters on a white wall.
It falls straight down rather than diagonally. A diagonal throw
is a shadow cast by an object standing off a surface, which is
what the cards on the other packs are; these letters are not
standing off anything, and at 40px an offset in both axes reads
as an emboss rather than as depth. Three pixels down and sixteen
of blur is enough to find an edge under every stem without the
blur becoming visible as grey.
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered TWICE - once for
the letters and once for the words picked out of them (see
editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists, so a row of
three is a row of three.
This is the first pack anywhere to state `highlight`, and the
reason it needs it is the reason `colors` in js/channels.js is
worth reading first. On every other palette here the picked words
are a different CUT of the same face in the same colour, so
`text` reaches them too and there is one question. Here the
picked words are a different colour as well as a different face,
and which one is the user's - so there are two questions, and a
pack that states the second list is saying exactly that. Left
unstated, the highlight would follow the block and a picked word
would come out the same white as its neighbours in a face most
people would not notice at a glance.
The same three in both lists, in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is
the PAIRING, and two rows written the same way read as one
palette offered twice rather than as two unrelated sets. What it
is FOR here is one step more literal than usual - the highlight
is meant to be whichever of the three the block is not, so the
second row is the first row asked again.
The two warm colours are the brand and the white is the ground
they are read against. #FF3131 is the hot one and #FF914D the
warm one, and they are far enough apart to be told apart at
caption size on a phone while both being legible on the same dark
band - which is the whole of what this palette asks of a colour,
since either can be the block or the picked word.
Nine combinations, and three of them set a picked word in exactly
the colour of its neighbours, which leaves the change of face as
the only difference. Nothing stops the user choosing one and that
is not an oversight: the two lists are independent because the
pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the three matching
combinations would cost the panel more explaining than a quiet
highlight costs the user, who can see it is quiet and presses
another swatch.
There is no `panel` list, because there is no panel. That row of
buttons is simply not drawn rather than drawn dead - see
editor.paletteOf, which hides a row whose colours would recolour
something the channel never puts on the canvas.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Garet Book, in a colour of its own that
the user chooses from the second row of swatches.
Two changes at once, where every sibling makes one. Those packs
put their captions on a card, and a card is a flat ground where a
change of weight or of slant alone is as loud as anything needs
to be. This one puts them on a photograph under a shade, and a
photograph is busy: a picked word that differs only in the shape
of its letters is a word most viewers will not notice, because
there is grain and edge and detail competing with exactly that
signal. Colour is what carries across a busy ground, and the face
is what makes the change deliberate rather than a recolour
somebody applied.
Garet against Open Sans is a geometric against a humanist - one
built on circles with a single-storey a, the other drawn from
handwriting with a two-storey one. That is a change of VOICE and
not a change of emphasis, which is the right relation here for
Laugh Society 2's reason: the picked word reads as somebody else
speaking rather than as the same voice under a light. It is also
why it is not simply a bolder Open Sans - a weight is the same
voice louder, and on a busy ground it is the change least likely
to survive.
The default is #FF3131 while the block's is white, and the two
differing is the point rather than an accident of listing. The
same colour in both rows would leave a picked word separated by
the face alone on an untouched frame, which is the one case this
channel is careful not to produce - and it would make the second
row of swatches look like a copy of the first rather than a
question with its own answer. Red on white is also the pairing
this show opens on; the other eight are a button away.
Word scope, the same as every neighbour, and for their reason: a
caption's line breaks are wherever the sentence happened to run
out of width, so picking a line out picks out a fragment rather
than a thought. The words are what carry meaning, and the one
worth setting apart - a name, a number, the verb the clip turns
on - sits in the middle of a line as often as it fills one. A row
whose picked words are in another face is built out of runs, each
measured and drawn in its own face at the pen the runs before it
reached (see `runRows` in js/text.js), which is what lets the
face change at a word and costs the kerning across each join.
Mode is colour rather than box, which on this channel is not the
usual argument. Elsewhere it is that the words are already on a
solid ground and there is nothing to box against; here it is that
a box would be the card this channel deliberately does not have,
drawn one word at a time.
The shadow is stated rather than inherited, and stated as the
same one the unhighlighted words carry above, to the number - so
every word lifts off the picture the same way whether it is
picked out or not. The skeleton's own highlight shadow is a
wider, softer, centred one meant to sit under a filled box, and
it would put a picked word at a different depth from the words
either side of it on the same line.
_comment_panel: There is none, and its absence is this channel's whole design -
see `_comment_title` and `_comment_scrim` above. Left out rather
than written as null, because the skeleton's answer is already
null and a key restating it would read as a slab somebody had
switched off rather than as a channel that never had one.
_comment_movable: The block starts at the foot of the frame and the user moves it
from there. Same reasoning as on every channel beside this one:
the bottom of a captured still is only where a caption usually
belongs, and it lands over somebody's face often enough that
being able to drag it clear is part of the job.
One thing is different, and it is worth knowing before dragging
far. On those channels the caption carries its own ground with it
- the card moves where the words move, so a block dragged to the
top of the frame is as legible there as it was at the foot. Here
the ground is the scrim, and the scrim does not move: it is a
shade on the bottom third of the picture, not a shape behind the
type. A block dragged above it keeps its drop shadow and nothing
else. That is a real limit rather than a bug - the drag is there
to clear a face by a line or two, and a caption that has to live
at the top of the frame is a frame this channel is the wrong one

_comment: Hall of Femme's block, stated in its numbers: nearly the full
width, standing on a margin off the bottom edge that clears a
player's own furniture, at a stated 40px so that forty stills
cut from one video are one set rather than forty type sizes.
What each of them is doing there, and what a stated
`fontSize` switches off, is written out in that pack and in
`fontSize` in js/channels.js.
Keeping them unchanged is the point rather than laziness.
This channel differs from its neighbours in how the words are
SET - the face, the colours, the ground under them - and not
in where they sit or how big they are, which are facts about
Snapchat's frame rather than about any show. It is also what
makes the scrim's third of the frame the right third: those
numbers are what the arithmetic in `_comment_scrim` is done
against, so changing one of them means recomputing the shade.
`maxChars` is the second ceiling on where the lines break -
the width asks what the frame holds, this asks what a viewer
reads at a glance, and a line has to be under both. It is the
same twenty every pack under this heading states, and it is
the ceiling that usually binds here: Open Sans's lower-case
is narrower than the capitals most siblings break against, so
twenty characters of it sit well inside the column and
without this the lines would run past thirty.
`freeform` on, and four lines, because a caption is a
sentence rather than three typed beats - it arrives already
broken (see js/caption.js) into one text box the user rewraps
by hand. Four is a count of slots and a freeform channel has
none, so it does nothing here; it is stated because four
lines is what the scrim was measured against.
lineGap is not stated, so the lines are spaced by the
renderer's own 10px (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE in js/channels.js).
On the panelled packs that number has to be read twice over,
because a joined slab changes what it measures between; with
no slab here it is simply the gap between two lines of type,
which is what it says.
maxBlockHeightRatio no longer decides the caption's size, and
no longer pulls a block in either - a size the renderer may
shrink is not a stated size. It is left where every sibling
leaves it, and on this channel it is the one number in the
block genuinely doing nothing: those packs at least spend it
on the card's padding (see BLOCK_BUDGET in js/text.js), and
there is no card here to spend it on.

_comment_branding: `gradient` is true, and on this channel it means the SCRIM above
rather than the backend's dark gradient - the same thing it means on
Laugh Society 2, and the reason the two are one button is that they
are one idea: the shade that holds the title legible. It arrives on
because the shade is part of how this channel looks rather than an
effect to go and find, and the button turns it off for the frame
whose picture is already dark enough to carry white type unaided.
Every other channel under this heading sets `gradient` false, and
each of them says why: the backend's gradient exists to hold a title
legible against the photograph, and their titles are on a slab of
their own. This channel's title IS on the photograph, so it needs
that job doing - and does it itself.
This is also the first pack that both draws the photograph and
states a scrim, and it is what forced state.backendPresentation into
existence. The two gradients are not alike: the backend's is a
full-height ramp down the SIDE the title sits on, put there to clear
a column for a headline beside a subject, and baked into the pixels
it returns. Asked for on top of the scrim it would darken a vertical
still down one edge as well as up from the foot - two shades, in two
directions, for one press of one button. So a channel with a scrim
is now never asked for the backend's; Laugh Society 2 was covered by
accident before, since a channel that never draws the photograph
cannot show what was done to it.
